title: Building nuclear’s next-gen workforce
html:
As the nuclear energy industry advances a new generation of more cost-effective, more efficient small reactors, another challenge is coming into sharper focus: Who will build, operate, and maintain them?

The Department of Energy projects that the nuclear energy sector will need more than 375,000 skilled workers by 2050 to sustain existing nuclear power operations and support deployment of next-gen reactors. Meeting that demand will require a workforce pipeline that begins well before someone walks through the doors of a nuclear facility for the first time.

The Nuclear Energy Academic Roadmap (NEAR) was created to address the critical need for a skilled nuclear energy workforce.

Developed as a collaborative effort of the Partnership for Nuclear Energy, an Oak Ridge Associated Universities (ORAU)–led nationwide public-private partnership, NEAR brings together universities, community colleges, technical training organizations, nuclear industry companies, professional organizations, national laboratories, and government agencies to create a blueprint for strengthening nuclear education and workforce development.

Michelle Goodson, ORAU senior director for strategic growth and partnerships, stressed that the road map “is not just a document—it’s a blueprint for our future” that is being taken from theory to action.

“By bridging educational gaps and creating clear pathways for emerging talent, we are investing in the next generation of nuclear professionals,” she said.

NEAR was unveiled at the Nuclear Energy Conference and Expo in Atlanta, Ga., in September 2025. Michelle Goodson, ORAU senior director for strategic growth and partnerships (right), was on a panel that included (from left) ANS past president Lisa Marshall, SueMagidson of Vanderbilt University, Sola Talabi of Pittsburgh Technical, and Lyn Potter of Chattanooga State Community College. (Photo: ORAU)

From recommendations to results

NEAR identified more than 70 recommendations spanning the education and workforce-development continuum and organized them into four strategic priority areas:

Enhancing nuclear career awareness, which informs people about various jobs, career paths, and earning potential. It aids students in choosing careers in the nuclear industry and helps employees find growth opportunities.

Supporting pipeline and pathway development, which aims to boost the number and diversity of workers and create pathways linking students and workers to higher education and job opportunities.

Identifying financial support, resources, and programs, which helps remove financial barriers from the pursuit of careers in the nuclear field and guarantees the continuity and effectiveness of educational programs.

Optimizing academic resources through collaboration, which involves sharing adaptable educational coursework and tools, equipment, and facilities among learning institutions to save time and money while ensuring consistent learning experiences across various educational settings.

Laura Hammons, ORAU senior program manager for strategic nuclear workforce development, said that NEAR “brings stakeholders to the table who can work together. We say it all the time, but collaboration is so important.”

That philosophy is becoming one of the initiative’s defining characteristics. “The question is no longer simply, ‘What needs to change?’ but ‘Who can help us do it?’” Hammons said.

In answer to that question, Hammons pointed to a small group of stakeholders who were involved in the development of NEAR and have now stepped forward to lead or co-lead work connected to each of the road map’s four pillars.

While some recommendations are relatively straightforward to advance and progress is being made quickly—especially in the career awareness pillar—other recommendations, like those involving financial resources and systemic change, are more complex and will take more effort to implement.

The career awareness group was able to narrow 20 or so recommendations down to six priorities, each with a specific project implementation plan.

For instance, one project focuses on implementation of the Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Career Cluster, a standalone national career and technical education framework launched by the Center for Energy Workforce Development.

The ENR Cluster already has been adopted by more than 30 states, but now the focus is on implementation, which can be especially challenging in K-12 education, according to Hammons, given competing priorities and crowded schedules.

“Adding another curriculum—even one as valuable and needed like nuclear energy—can be difficult if educators are expected to determine on their own how to fit it into their classrooms. Shoehorning another curriculum is a challenge in and of itself,” Hammons said.

The solution under development is a practical turnkey implementation guide that would provide the resources and steps educators need to put the new curriculum into practice. There are plans to develop a companion piece specifically for industry that will guide school systems on how to make the right requests and help industry to understand how best to support the future workforce as students move through the educational system.

Meanwhile, the pipeline and pathway development team is looking at specific project plans for education initiatives, broadening access to training, and improving communication.

Nuclear energy needs all workers

Ashley Stowe (right), ORAU chief growth and partnerships officer, led a panel discussion during the Pathway to Trades Summit in May 2026 on ORAU’s main campus in Oak Ridge, Tenn. The summit addressed the challenge of building a skilled workforce capable of meeting the rapidly growing demands of the nuclear sector. (Photo: ORAU)

It’s not just engineers, technicians, and scientists who keep the nuclear sector running. Skilled trades workers like electricians, welders, plumbers, carpenters, steelworkers, and others are critical to building, maintaining, and operating nuclear energy facilities.

NEAR recognizes that the skilled trades need improved career awareness. They also need stronger education and training pipelines and pathways. Prospective skilled tradespeople can face financial and resource barriers, and hiring well-qualified workers depends on partnerships and collaborations among employers, schools, and other organizations to meet workforce demand.

This was the impetus behind ORAU’s inaugural Pathway to Trades Summit, held in Oak Ridge, Tenn., in May, hosted in collaboration with North America’s Building Trades Unions and the Tennessee Nuclear Network.

The summit brought together leaders from labor organizations, industry, government, education, and community support services for a day of conversations and collaboration to identify priorities and take steps to building a skilled workforce capable of meeting the demands of the nuclear sector.

Speaking out on nuclear workforce issues are (from left) Lori Brady, a program manager at the Nuclear Energy Institute, moderating a NEAR panel at the joint ANS-NEI Nuclear Energy Conference and Expo in Atlanta, Ga., in September 2025; Michelle Scott, acting deputy assistant secretary for strategic crosscuts in the DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy, addressing the audience at the Pathway to Trades Summit in Oak Ridge, Tenn., in May 2026; and Meghan Millwood, ORAU president and CEO, also addressing Pathway to Trades Summit attendees. (Photos: ORAU)

Just the beginning

NEAR was developed with contributions from people across academia, industry, and government. ORAU supported the effort, but the expertise came from the people around the table—many of whom continue to volunteer their time to advance the work.

“There is no single organization that can build the nuclear workforce the country will need over the next several decades,” Goodson said. “It will take educators, employers, government agencies, universities, community colleges, technical training organizations, national laboratories, industry associations, and communities working together to meet this critical need.”

Hammons is pleased to see forward movement in NEAR, with career awareness and pathway development recommendations moving toward implementation and work on financial resources and collaborative academic resources advancing. Still, the invitation is open to interested stakeholders who want to get involved in NEAR.

“Tell us what you’re already doing or how you want to get involved, share any resources you’ve developed, and join people working to turn recommendations into action,” Hammons said.

Michael Holtz is a senior communications and marketing specialist for ORAU.

To get involved in NEAR, contact Laura Hammons at [email protected].
